patient.chief_complaint: Five months of sleepiness, amnesia and apathy since an admission for unexplained drowsiness
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Beatrice Sartori is a 66-year-old hospital pharmacy technician who five months ago became profoundly drowsy and confused over the course of an hour at work. She was admitted, a CT of the head was reported as normal, routine bloods and a toxicology screen were unremarkable, and after three days of gradual improvement she was discharged with a diagnosis of probable encephalopathy of uncertain cause and a hypnotic for presumed sleep disturbance. Her husband reports that she has never returned to normal. She sleeps twelve to fourteen hours a night and dozes repeatedly during the day, but rouses immediately and fully when spoken to. She cannot retain anything new: she asks the same question repeatedly, cannot remember whether she has taken her tablets, and has twice told her daughter news she had been told the day before as though it were fresh. She is strikingly unconcerned about all of it. She has not returned to work, where she dispensed medication. Her husband has also noticed that she 'does not look up' — she cannot see items on a high shelf without tilting her head. There has been no further abrupt event, no headache, no weakness, no hallucinations and no dream enactment.

vascular_cognitive_impairment.summary: No disease-modifying therapy exists for vascular cognitive impairment; management is control of the vascular risk factors, secondary prevention matched to the mechanism, review of the anticholinergic burden, and treatment of coexisting Alzheimer pathology where biomarkers support it.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Vascular dementia — strategic infarct type, bilateral paramedian thalamic and rostral midbrain infarction in the artery of Percheron territory

differential.key_features: This was the discharge diagnosis and it survived because the CT was normal; a fixed deficit five months later with a vertical gaze palsy and a storage amnesia is an anatomical lesion, not a resolved metabolic disturbance

differential.diagnosis: Idiopathic hypersomnia or a sleep disorder
differential.key_features: The hypnotic prescribed at discharge treats this hypothesis, but hypersomnolence with a storage amnesia and a supranuclear vertical gaze palsy is a diencephalic lesion, and the drug can only worsen it
Onset was abrupt on a single day with no progression in five months, the hippocampi are entirely normal and language and working memory are preserved
A vertical gaze palsy with apathy overlaps, but onset was abrupt, there is no axial rigidity, no falls, no midbrain atrophy, and there has been no progression

Confabulation and amnesia overlap, but there is no alcohol or nutritional risk, no ophthalmoparesis of the nuclear type, and the lesions are ischaemic in a defined arterial territory with normal mamillary bodies

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; it belongs to the differential of a rapidly progressive or fluctuating course (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, non-convulsive status, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy), none of which is present here

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cardiac sympathetic imaging is a test for dementia with Lewy bodies and for autonomic failure; it says nothing about cerebrovascular disease

An untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery in a chronic stepwise decline with a hypertensive imaging burden is the archetypal expensive miss; the indication for those assays is a subacute multidomain syndrome
The MRI already obtained answers everything a CT could and more: CT cannot show microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis, so it cannot grade the vascular burden this diagnosis rests on
There is no embolic lesion pattern to explain: the burden here is small-vessel, and a structural cardioembolic source would not account for it
Prolonged rhythm monitoring is for an unexplained embolic infarct pattern; in pure small-vessel disease it changes nothing about the diagnosis or the treatment

sequence_constraints.reason: Document the cognitive deficit before attributing it: imaging read without a cognitive profile invites over-attribution of incidental white matter change

critical_actions: Recognise that a fixed deficit five months after an abrupt event is a structural lesion, not a resolved encephalopathy
Examine vertical gaze and test the vestibulo-ocular reflex — a supranuclear vertical gaze palsy localises to the midbrain-diencephalic junction
Test recognition memory to establish a storage deficit
Obtain MRI: paramedian thalamic infarcts are characteristically invisible on CT, as they were during the index admission
Obtain angiography to demonstrate the artery of Percheron variant, which explains bilateral infarction from a single occlusion
Stop the hypnotic prescribed for presumed sleep disturbance, which worsens both the hypersomnolence and the amnesia
Address the occupational risk explicitly: she dispensed medication and cannot do so with this deficit
contraindicated_actions: Do not accept a normal CT as excluding bilateral paramedian thalamic infarction
Do not prescribe or continue a hypnotic in a patient with hypersomnolence from a diencephalic lesion and a dense amnesia
Do not carry forward a diagnosis of 'encephalopathy of uncertain cause' when a fixed anatomical syndrome is present
Do not rely on the patient's own account when apathy and amnesia are both present
Do not clear her to return to dispensing medication without formal occupational assessment
key_reasoning_points: The triad localises: hypersomnolence, a dense storage amnesia and a supranuclear vertical gaze palsy together point to the paramedian thalami and rostral midbrain, and the artery of Percheron is the vessel that supplies all three in one territory
A single anatomical variant explains a bilateral lesion from a single occlusion, which is why the syndrome looks diffuse and is in fact focal
1.6 mL of tissue produced a dementia — the strategic principle in its clearest form, because the dorsomedial nuclei and mamillothalamic tracts carry the memory circuit bilaterally
CT misses paramedian thalamic infarcts, and a normal CT is what allowed five months and an inappropriate hypnotic to intervene
Preserved arousability distinguishes a diencephalic hypersomnolence from a reduced level of consciousness, and it is what makes this a chronic focal syndrome rather than an encephalopathy

red_herrings.data_point: A normal head CT during the index admission and a discharge diagnosis of encephalopathy
red_herrings.intended_effect: Excludes a structural lesion and leaves a metabolic label that was never revisited
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Paramedian thalamic infarcts are characteristically invisible on CT; the MRI shows chronic bilateral thalamic and midbrain infarction dating to that admission
